content.intro: This lesson focuses on advanced release engineering. Advanced release engineering coordinates candidate validation, compatibility checks, changelog generation, versioning, publication, and rollback ownership. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.

items.title: Version compatibility checks
items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

content_blocks.code:
name: Prepare tagged release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*.*.*"]
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Create release notes from tag
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: gh release create "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --generate-notes
content_blocks.expected_output: A matching tag triggers the GitHub CLI release creation command. This requires an authorized token and a valid tag, so use only a controlled test release.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Test with a disposable repository/tag and confirm the `gh` CLI is available on the selected runner; inspect current permission requirements.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Do not run against production tags until tag protection, authorization, release notes, and rollback policy are configured.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Advanced release engineering coordinates candidate validation, compatibility checks, changelog generation, versioning, publication, and rollback ownership. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
